title: The Living Space: Psychological Well-Being and Mental Health in Response to Interiors Presented in Virtual Reality
research_question: To systematically examine the influence of contrasting contours (angular versus curved) in virtual indoor architectural settings on affect, behavior, and cognition, and to explore the impact of architectural style (modern vs. classic) as a second-level variable.

participants.description: 48 healthy adults (aged 18-40 years, M=27.71, 25F/16M for ASE/MAS; M=27.31, 23F/13M for PRS; M=27.55, 27F/15M for CT) were enrolled, with 36-42 included in analyses depending on the measure. 85.36% born in Germany, fluent in German, no severe visual impairments, diagnosed mental or neurodegenerative disorder, or cognitive impairment.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through the Castellum Database of the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin (MPIB) and an online platform (ebay-kleinanzeigen.de).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four photorealistic virtual 3D living rooms (Angular Modern, Curved Modern, Angular Classic, Curved Classic) were created. Rooms within each pair were identical except for contour (angular vs. curved window openings, furniture, fixtures, accessories). The main contrast between pairs was architectural style (modern vs. classic), differing in layout, furniture components, and materials. Classic rooms included biophilic design elements (wood, plants, green color). All rooms had identical boundaries, ceiling, floor, door/window locations, main seating positions, main light, primary color (green), and a natural outdoor window view. Participants freely explored each room for 3 minutes.

measures.instrument: 20 bipolar items (e.g., pleasantness, beauty, novelty, order, harmony, spaciousness, enclosure, warmth) on 11-point numeric scales (-5 to 5).
11 dimensions (e.g., shame, fear, happiness, alertness, tension, activity) on 11-point intensity rating scales (0 to 10 or -5 to 5).
Adapted 12-item German version of the Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS), with 4 subscales (fascination, being away, coherence, scope) on a 5-point Likert scale (0 to 4).
In-VR two-minute skip counting task (subtracting 13 from a 4-digit number). Score calculated as correct answers / total attempts.
Adapted German version of the Simulation Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), 16 items on a 4-point Likert scale (0 to 3), yielding Nausea, Oculomotor, Disorientation subscores, and a Total Score.
iGroup Presence Questionnaire (IPQ), 14 items on a 5-point Likert scale (1 to 5), yielding General Presence, Spatial Presence, Involvement, and Experienced Realism subscales.

findings.mechanism: Angular forms may be perceived as more novel, potentially due to less common exposure or higher prediction error compared to curved forms in certain contexts.
Angular forms may be associated with higher perceived order, possibly due to their clear, predictable lines and geometric regularity.
Initial significance for curved rooms being more harmonious did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
Initial significance for angular rooms being more symmetrical did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
Initial significance for curved rooms being more exciting did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
No significant effects of contour were found on any dimensions of momentary affective state, with Bayesian factors indicating anecdotal to moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.
findings.quote: Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not find any effects of contour on momentary affective states.

findings.mechanism: No significant effect of contour was found on self-reported restored attention, with Bayesian factors indicating anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis.
findings.quote: There was no difference in self-reported restored attention after having been immersed in angular compared to curved rooms

findings.mechanism: No significant effect of contour was found on cognitive performance, with Bayesian factors indicating moderate evidence for the null hypothesis. The stress induced by the task might have overlapped potential effects of contours.
findings.quote: we found no effect of contour (Z = −0.43, p = 0.667) or room style (Z = 0.59, p = 0.552) on cognitive performance.

findings.mechanism: Initial significance for modern rooms being more spacious did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
Initial significance for classic rooms being more enclosed did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
Modern architectural styles, being more recent, are perceived as more novel compared to classic styles.
Modern architectural styles, following a 'less is more' principle, are perceived as more simple compared to classic styles with more ornamentation.
Initial significance for modern rooms being more ordered did not survive FDR correction, suggesting no robust effect in this context.
Classic rooms, potentially due to their materials or color palette, were perceived as warmer. This effect survived a less stringent FDR correction.
No significant effects of style were found on any dimensions of momentary affective state, with Bayesian factors indicating anecdotal to moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.
findings.quote: Similarly, there was no effect of style on momentary affective state

findings.mechanism: No significant effect of style was found on self-reported restored attention, with Bayesian factors indicating moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.
findings.quote: nor in modern compared to classic rooms—t(35) = −0.94, p = 0.352.

findings.mechanism: No significant effect of style was found on cognitive performance, with Bayesian factors indicating moderate evidence for the null hypothesis. The stress induced by the task might have overlapped potential effects of style.
findings.quote: we found no effect of contour (Z = −0.43, p = 0.667) or room style (Z = 0.59, p = 0.552) on cognitive performance.

findings.mechanism: The extended duration of the VR session led to a significant increase in self-reported cybersickness symptoms.
findings.quote: A paired sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated a significant increase of the overall cybersickness symptoms experienced by participants (Z = 4.5423, p < 0.001)

findings.mechanism: Males performed better than females in the cognitive task when exposed to angular rooms.
findings.quote: when looking solely at angular rooms, males performed better than females in the cognitive task.

findings.consequent: positive affect and spatial dimensions (6 out of 20)
findings.mechanism: Males rated angular rooms higher than females on six affective and spatial dimensions and reported higher positive affect after exploring them.
findings.quote: Additionally, they rated those rooms higher than females on six out of the 20 affective and spatial dimensions, and reported higher scores on positive affect after exploring them.

mechanisms: The psychological response to indoor design is complex and cannot be reduced to a generalized effect of contour or style, involving multifaceted layers that affect judgment on individual and contextual levels.
Previous findings of curvature preference fading with extended viewing time or immediate response instructions suggest an influence of meaning and semantic content on preference.
Response bias as a function of presentation order in lengthy sequential preference judgments may explain inconsistencies with prior research.
Cultural and individual differences (e.g., sex, expertise, background) between populations may contribute to inconsistent findings across studies.
The neglect of human movement's influence on spatial experience in studies using static stimuli limits the generalizability of findings.
Long evaluation times and numerous questions may lead to a 'museum-fatigue effect', impacting self-report reliability.
Stress induced by the cognitive task may have masked potential effects of environmental contours or style on performance.
Differences in color palette between modern and classic styles could confound perceived warmth ratings.
implementation_implications: A better understanding of human-environment interaction can inform design strategies to optimize psychological well-being and mental health.
Future research should focus on implicit measures of emotions, less stress-inducing cognitive tasks, and a more positive set of emotions.
Future studies should include equally sized sex groups to explore potential gender differences in architectural perception.
Future studies should aim at maximizing control for confounding variables by providing well-matched high and low-level properties when investigating architectural style.

tables.description: Results of statistical analyses (frequentist and Bayesian) for contour conditions (angular vs. curved) on momentary affective state, affective and spatial experience, perceived restorativeness, and cognitive task scores.

Results of statistical analyses (frequentist and Bayesian) for style conditions (modern vs. classic) on momentary affective state, affective and spatial experience, perceived restorativeness, and cognitive task scores.

limitations: The study's long evaluation time (3 min exploration + 9 min tasks/self-reports per room) and numerous questions (31 per room) may have caused a 'museum-fatigue effect', potentially impacting responses.
The stress-inducing nature of the cognitive task might have masked the subtle effects of environmental contours.
The sample was not balanced in terms of sex (more females than males), which could affect the generalizability of post-hoc sex-related findings.
The MAS scale's broad range of negative emotions might have been too general, suggesting future studies focus more on positive emotions.
The slight difference in color palette between modern and classic styles could be a confounding factor for perceived warmth.

The inclusion of biophilic features in classic rooms did not impact ratings of naturalness or perceived restorativeness, suggesting these elements might not have been sufficiently impactful or were confounded by other factors.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: There has been a recent interest in how architecture affects mental health and psychological well-being, motivated by the fact that we spend the majority of our waking time inside and interacting with built environments. Some studies have investigated the psychological responses to indoor design parameters; for instance, contours, and proposed that curved interiors, when compared to angular ones, were aesthetically preferred and induced higher positive emotions. The present study aimed to systematically examine this hypothesis and further explore the impact of contrasting contours on affect, behavior, and cognition. We exposed 42 participants to four well-matched indoor living rooms under a free-exploration photorealistic virtual reality paradigm. We included style as an explorative second-level variable. Out of the 33 outcome variables measured, and after correcting for false discoveries, only two eventually confirmed differences in the contours analysis, in favor of angular rooms. Analysis of style primarily validated the contrast of our stimulus set, and showed significance in one other dependent variable. Results of additional analysis using the Bayesian framework were in line with those of the frequentist approach. The present results provide evidence against the hypothesis that curvature is preferred, suggesting that the psychological response to contours in a close-to-reality architectural setting could be more complex. This study, therefore, helps to communicate a more complete scientific view on the experience of interior spaces and proposes directions for necessary future research.
